'''''Sideroxylon inerme''''' ('''aMasethole''' or '''white milkwood''', {{langx|af|wit-melkhout}}, {{langx|xh|Ximafana}}, {{langx|zu|Umakhwelafingqane}})<ref name="dwaf">{{cite web
 |url         = http://www2.dwaf.gov.za/dwaf/cmsdocs/4116___poster%20protected%20trees.pdf
 |title       = Protected Trees
 |date        = 3 May 2013
 |publisher   = Department of Water Affairs and Forestry, Republic of South Africa
 |url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20100705085122/http://www2.dwaf.gov.za/dwaf/cmsdocs/4116___poster%20protected%20trees.pdf
 |archive-date = 5 July 2010
}}</ref> is a southern and eastern African coastal tree, with dense foliage, black berries and small, foetid, greenish flowers. The tree's generic name means "Iron-wood" in Greek, referring to its very hard timber.

It is one of [[South Africa]]'s "Protected Trees" and several specimens are [[Provincial heritage site (South Africa)|provincial heritage sites]].<ref name="bosman">[http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantqrs/sideroxinerm.htm '' Sideroxylon inerme''] in Freddie Bosman' site, from the Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden.</ref> This is the only member of the genus ''Sideroxylon'' in Southern Africa.

==Distribution==
[[File:Sideroxylon inerme South African Milkwood habit IMG 4863.JPG|thumb|left|Cape milkwood trees in typical coastal habitat]]
''Sideroxylon inerme'' trees are scattered through the coastal woodlands and littoral forests of southern and eastern Africa, from the [[Cape Provinces]] of South Africa in the south to [[Somalia]] in the north, and on [[Aldabra]], the [[Comoro Islands]], and the [[Mozambique Channel Islands]] in the western Indian Ocean.<ref name = powo/> Historically, dense forests of large milkwood trees used to exist along the coast and bays of [[Cape Town]], especially at [[Noordhoek, Cape Town|Noordhoek]], Macassar and Gordons Bay.
The milkwood is not endangered but it is one of South Africa's [[Protected Tree]]s, which means that it is illegal to damage, move or destroy them.<ref name="bosman"/>

==Description==
''Sideroxylon inerme'' is a semi-coastal sturdy broadleaf [[Evergreen|evergreen tree]] with dense foliage, displays of white bisexual flowers and edible purplish-black berries. It boasts leathery, spiral leaves, which, like the berries, contain [[Latex|milky latex]]. Young branches and new leaves are always covered with fine hairs. The tree can reach 15 m.{{cn|date=June 2023}}

The milkwood has considerable value in traditional medicine and attracts birds, monkeys and other animals to its flowers and fruits : [[Speckled mousebird]]s eat the flowers ; birds, [[bat]]s, [[monkey]]s and [[bush pig]]s eat the fruit. It is also an effective [[firebreak]] and is cultivated for that purpose.<ref name="bosman"/>

==Subspecies==
''Sideroxylon inerme'' includes three subspecies:<ref name = powo/>
* ''Sideroxylon inerme'' subsp. ''cryptophlebium'' (Baker) J.H.Hemsl., which grows on [[Aldabra Group|Aldabra island]] ([[Seychelles]]);
* ''Sideroxylon inerme'' subsp. ''diospyroides'' (Baker) J.H.Hemsl., whose range extends to [[Somalia]], [[Kenya]], [[Tanzania]], [[Zimbabwe]] and [[Mozambique]] ;
* ''Sideroxylon inerme'' subsp. ''inerme'', in [[Mozambique]] and [[South Africa]].<ref name="prota-side">[http://www.prota4u.org/protav8.asp?fr=1&h=M4&t=Sideroxylon,inerme&p=Sideroxylon+inerme#Synonyms ''Sideroxylon inerme''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120530110821/http://www.prota4u.org/protav8.asp?fr=1&h=M4&t=Sideroxylon,inerme&p=Sideroxylon+inerme |date=2012-05-30 }} in PROTA4U site, a database and use guide for African plants.</ref>

==Historical aspects==
[[File:Photo 5 Treaty Tree. Cnr Treaty and Spring St, Woodstock. Cape Town..JPG|thumb|275px|The "Treaty Tree" in Woodstock, [[Cape Town]].]]
The white milkwood has great significance in South Africa's heritage, with three specimens proclaimed as [[Provincial heritage site (South Africa)|provincial heritage sites]]:  
* The '''[[Post Office Tree]]''' in [[Mossel Bay]] is believed to be 600 years old. The Post Office tree, which still stands about 1000 feet from Santos Beach, is considered the first  (unofficial) post office in South Africa. It was declared a [[Provincial heritage site (South Africa)|provincial heritage site]] in 1938 and is marked with a plaque reading: “This post office tree stands near the fountains where the Portuguese navigators regularly drew water at Aguada de São Bras (now Mossel Bay) from 1488 onwards. In May 1500 [[Pêro de Ataíde]], captain of a homeward-bound ship of [[Pedro Cabral|Pedro Cabral’s]] fleet, left a message here which was found on 7 July 1507 by the outward bound ships of [[João da Nova]]. According to tradition the message was placed in an old shoe and tied to a tree”. The seven-year-old letter described the loss at sea of four ships from the expedition of [[Bartolomeu Dias]], and warned of hostilities encountered on the Indian coast. In 1962 [[South African Post Office|SAPO]], the South African postal service, erected a mailbox at the tree in the shape of a shoe, and items posted from there are cancelled with a special stamp.<ref name=psa>{{cite web|title=The Portuguese in South Africa|url=http://ancestry24.com/the-portuguese-in-south-africa/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101212144714/http://ancestry24.com/the-portuguese-in-south-africa/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=December 12, 2010|publisher=ancestor24.com|access-date=10 January 2013}}</ref>
* The '''[[Treaty Tree]]''' in [[Woodstock, Cape Town]] stood next to the house where in 1806 the [[Batavian Republic]] (the modern [[Netherlands]]) [[Battle of Blaauwberg|surrendered Cape Town]] to the British.
* The '''Fingo Milkwood''' in the [[Eastern Cape]] was the location where in 1835 the [[Fengu people]] signed a treaty of alliance with the [[Cape Colony]].
* The ''Grandfather of Still Bay'' is estimated to be about 1000 years old. It was entered into the register of [[List of Champion Trees (South Africa)|Champion Trees]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=STILBAAI'S SPECIAL MILKWOOD TREE |url=https://mystilbaai.co.za/stilbaais-special-milkwood-tree/ |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=My Stilbaai.co.za Business Restaurant Accommodation Tourism Guide Southern Cape |language=en-US}}</ref>
